newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan says fighting is well south of key town.
newsitem.headline: Sudan says fighting is well south of key town.

text.p: The Sudanese army battled attacking forces in the east Sudanese province of Blue Nile on Monday but the army and rebels gave conflicting accounts of the rebel campaign to take the important town of Damazin.

The attacks began along the Ethiopian border eight days ago when the rebels, an alliance of northern and southern groups, launched a big offensive designed to pave the way for a popular uprising in the capital Khartoum.
The Sudanese government says it is under attack mainly from Ethiopian and Eritrean forces but all the other parties say this is just an attempt to win international sympathy.
A Sudanese army spokesman denied an opposition report that the rebels wiped out an army detachment of about 150 men on Sunday at Keili, 100 km (60 miles) south of Damazin.
But the spokesman, Lieutenant-General Mohammad al-Sanoussi Ahmed, said the army had lost one man killed and eight wounded in an attack on a reconnaissance patrol further north at Bikori.

In the Eritrean capital Asmara an opposition spokesman said the rebels had advanced to within 70 km (45 miles) of Damazin, the regional capital and the site of a hydroelectricity plant which supplies Khartoum with most of its power.
General Ahmed, asked how close to Damazin the front had reached, told a briefing: "It is far from Damazin. The nearest point is not less than 85 to 100 km (53 to 60 miles)."
"The most hot area now is the Blue Nile area...and now exactly we are fighting the Ethiopian troops," he added.
"All in all there is a division (of the Sudanese army) which has so many flanks that it is covering a front of not less than 130 km (80 miles)," the general added.
A division, which could have as many as 15,000 men, is a much larger military formation than suggested in previous reports on the conflict.
Islamist leader Hassan al-Turabi said last week the army originally had four battalions, or up to 4,000 men, in the area.

But the government has been sending convoys of army reinforcements down to Damazin, along with units of the paramilitary People's Defence Forces, the military wing of the Islamists who dominate the Sudanese government.
In the middle of last week both sides reported fighting further north around the town of Kassala, close to the Eritrean border, but the general said there was a lull on that front.
"As for the Eritrean area, now it is somewhat stable and our side now has the upper hand, although there are many pockets of Eritrean troops and mercenaries (rebels)," he said.
In Asmara Yassir Arman, spokesman for the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), told Reuters that the rebels of the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) were still advancing.
"We are moving towards Damazin. We are doing our best. Our plan is being executed successfully so far. We are confident of getting to Damazin," he added.
In Cairo, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak discussed the situation in neighbouring Sudan with senior ministers.
Information Minister Safwat Sherif said Mubarak reiterated that Egypt would not interfere in Sudan's internal affairs because the conflict was between the rulers and opposition forces.

"Egypt rejects completely any attempt to divide Sudan," added the minister. Egypt's main concern in Sudan is for the waters of the Nile and it fears that an independent state in southern Sudan could complicate water supplies.
Mubarak turned down a request for help in the east by Sudanese Vice-President al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh last week.
Saleh, meanwhile, arrived in Damascus from Saudi Arabia on Monday as part of a tour to brief Arab leaders on the conflict.
